rv.q: It’s hubristic behaviour that’s simply not backed up by the quality of the writing.
It’s a whiplash-inducing cop out.
Let’s hope these, and the other two plays still to be announced, are better than this.
It is hard to decipher what we are watching here – comedy, drama or a theatrical car crash in slow motion.
Unfortunately there’s not an ounce of subtlety in the script or Sandberg’s direction.

Hiring Noah Schnapp, Stranger Things’ tormented Will Byers, with his 4.2 million YouTube followers and Ivy League degree in entrepreneurship, to play wealth-affected, time-shifted teens Dylan and Todd is astute.

Everyone tries their best to lift the material which despite a rock solid premise and strong opening, meanders into surreal territory with clunkily-written linking scenes and the over-egged Reality TV segment.
We open on a busy set (that gets busier and busier, with some frankly terrifying prop work required from the cast) that speaks of late 90s wealth.
Unfortunately, the result is a missed opportunity to say anything thoughtful at all.
A script as mangled as this one left me with more questions than answers.
The frankly ludicrous sequencing of events thereafter undermines any attempt to develop a coherent theme.
Unfortunately, not even a lavish set by Charlie Corcoran can hide the fact that this is a tasteless, aimless, pointless piece of theatre.
It really feels like Affluenza is the victim of its own wealth of ideas; even so its central provocation about wealth and privilege remains a compelling one.
The problem is that not much is done with the idea dramatically.
Despite its promise with a fantastic cast and impressive set, Affluenza is ultimately a play that never quite reaches its peak.
A fascinating and apt concept that, like Dylan himself, never quite finds its purpose.
Ultimately, the foundations of a very strong play are there.
Ultimately, Affluenza is a somewhat frustrating experience, not because it lacks interesting ideas, but because it never quite knows what to do with them.
Affluenza latches onto plenty of hot-button subjects, but has remarkably little of substance to say about them, and no convincing way of saying it.
The family at the heart of Affluenza may be rich in terms of money, but the play is far from rich in terms of detail.
Affluenza is a frustrating night at the theatre because such an important premise is squandered.
Affluenza begins with a provocative premise and an intriguing moral question, but ultimately loses confidence in the very story it sets out to tell.
Affluenza is a play that struggles to achieve what it sets out to do, and seems quite indecisive of what it wants to be.
There are the makings of an exciting production in there, but sadly it never bubbles to the surface.
When so little of a play makes sense, it is hard to recommend it on any level.

The most interesting thing about the new play Schnapp from Netflix’s Stranger Things has chosen for his stage debut is the dramatic rug pull it executes at the beginning of its 2nd act transforming the audience’s perspective.
Affluenza is, in a word, frustrating not just because of its complex storyline but ultimately due to the execution.
Unfortunately, the play never quite brings these elements together into the cohesive piece it could be.
Ultimately, both the production and script show promise, but neither feels fully realised.
An intriguing question about the extent to which wealth and privilege can distort one's moral compass gets off to a good start before losing its way...
Affluenza feels like an experiment in how many different ways you can sabotage a single script...

Everything about it is dreadful: a thin plot, amateurish dialogue, a structure that falls apart from the beginning, and some of the most appalling acting I've seen in all these years as a critic — and as a viewer.

cn.t: Critics find this privilege drama a confused, tonally jarring mess that squanders a promising premise with baffling plot twists and amateurish execution. Noah Schnapp's stage debut can't salvage what many call one of the year's worst plays.
